# Phase 2 report: the v1 model

*Generated by `npm run report` from `data/register.json` and the committed PVGIS, Octopus and PVcalc snapshots. Do not edit by hand.*

This report compares replacing a gas boiler with a new one, or with an air source heat pump, each with or without roof solar, on the price cap and on two Octopus time-of-use tariffs, for a 1930s semi in London, with honest ranges. It then runs the gas boiler and the heat pump on all ten house types. The numbers are estimates for a typical house of each kind, not advice for any particular home, and not financial advice.

## At a glance

- **Replacing the gas boiler like for like** (the reference) costs £3,000 and £2,040 a year to run, central (£1,820 to £2,280).
- **A heat pump on the price cap** costs £5,400 after the grant and £1,940 a year to run (£1,660 to £2,260), and emits 970 kg of CO₂e a year against 2,790 kg. It pays back within its lifetime in 60% of samples (central: 13 years); in 30% it doesn’t, and in 10% it is cheaper up front but costs more to run.
- **The combination most often cheapest to run** is “Heat pump with solar, Agile”, in 100% of samples (with about ±1 percentage points of sampling noise). Cosy and Agile rows carry the [time-of-use caveats](#time-of-use-caveats): a smart controller, a warmer house that isn’t valued, carbon by the annual factor, 0% VAT on electricity in every payback year, and, for Agile, one past year of prices on typical weather.
- **The heat pump figures carry a stated bias in the heat pump’s favour.** The heat pump heats from 7 am to 11 pm every day and the boiler in SAP’s two periods on weekdays. On those two schedules the engine understates the heat pump’s space heat against the boiler’s by about 6.7 points, against the government’s Home Energy Model, so the heat pump’s running costs may be a little low and its savings a little high ([issue 15](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/15); see the [schedules ADR](../REFERENCE/decisions/2026-10-20-heating-schedules-one-thermal-mass-node.md)). The sensitivity section shows the heat pump on the gas schedule instead.

## The house

Semi-detached, cavity, 1930–49, in London (RdSAP age band C): 90 m² over 2 storeys, filled cavity walls, about 100 mm of loft insulation and double glazing installed before 2002, with 3 occupants. Every setup on every tariff runs on this house.

- **Geometry**, derived from the floor area and the footprint shape: 19.8 m of exposed perimeter, 84 m² of external wall and 17.9 m² of windows. The ground floor U-value is 0.66 W/m²K (BS EN ISO 13370, as RdSAP 10 applies it). Heat loss coefficient (central): 274 W/K.
- **Heating:** a setpoint of 17.6 °C air (central), calibrated so the gas boiler uses 13,200 kWh of gas a year. The boiler heats in SAP’s periods (weekdays 7–9 am and 4–11 pm, weekends 7 am to 11 pm); the heat pump from 7 am to 11 pm every day, SAP’s longer heat pump day. Between periods the house cools against its thermal mass. The heat pump’s output is capped at 1.15 × its design heat loss, the boiler’s at 24 kW.
- **Solar:** 3.85 kWp on one roof slope (central), facing south. Generation meets the house’s own use first; the rest is exported at 12.00p a kWh.
- **Prices:** gas is always on the Ofgem price cap for the London region, by Direct Debit, for 1 October–31 December 2026: 8.15p a kWh and 30.20p a day. Electricity is on the cap (26.60p a kWh and 42.92p a day), Octopus Cosy (14.12p to 43.19p a kWh by time of day, 42.29p a day; heat pump homes only) or Octopus Agile (a past year’s half-hourly rates, 37.65p a day). Electricity prices include VAT at 0%. A heat pump house has no gas supply, so it pays no gas standing charge.
- **Carbon:** 0.18231 kgCO₂e a kWh of gas and 0.14396 kgCO₂e a kWh of grid electricity (annual average).

The three shares sum to 100%.

## Time-of-use caveats

These apply to every Cosy and Agile result in this report.

- **Cosy and Agile results assume a smart controller** that follows the control rules. A heat pump left on its schedule costs what the “control off” rows show.
- **Control keeps the house warmer.** Preheating holds it above the setpoint in cheap hours, so Cosy and Agile buy extra warmth the comparison doesn’t value; the mean indoor temperatures show how much.
- **Carbon counts the extra electricity but not when it is used.** The annual grid factor can’t credit cheap hours that are often cleaner ([issue 17](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/17)).
- **Electricity carries no VAT from October 2026 to March 2027,** and every year of payback assumes it stays at 0% while gas carries 5%: a small tilt towards the heat pump.
- **“Cheapest on its tariff”** ranks 2 combinations on Cosy and 4 on the price cap and on Agile, so the shares don’t compare between tariffs.
- **Agile is one past year:** its half-hourly London rates from October 2025 to September 2026, placed on the typical year by calendar date and time. A past year is not a forecast.
- **Past prices on typical weather:** the year’s prices are paired with the typical year’s weather, which loses the link between price spikes and cold, still days. This likely flatters the heat pump on Agile.
- **Control knows each day’s prices in advance.** Octopus publishes them the day before, so this is realistic for a smart controller, but it favours the heat pump over a household that doesn’t respond.
- **Weekdays don’t match** between the past year and the reference year the schedules use.

What control does to the heat pump without solar, central. The shares are of the heat pump’s own electricity. With no control, the year’s mean indoor temperature is 18.2 °C for the heat pump on its schedule and 18.2 °C for the gas boiler on its own.

| Tariff and control | Mean indoor temperature | In cheap hours | In peak hours | Space heat | Heat pump electricity | Running cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Cosy, control off | 18.2 °C | 20% | 10% | 9,300 kWh | 4,200 kWh | £1,980 |
| Cosy, control on | 19.1 °C | 75% | 0% | 11,400 kWh | 4,900 kWh | £1,710 |
| Agile, control off | 18.2 °C | 10% | 35% | 9,300 kWh | 4,200 kWh | £1,450 |
| Agile, control on | 18.6 °C | 40% | 10% | 10,200 kWh | 4,500 kWh | £1,390 |

Control raises the setpoint in cheap hours and lowers it in peak hours during heating, and fills the cylinder in cheap hours; on the price cap it changes nothing ([engine.md](../REFERENCE/engine.md#tariffs-and-control)).

## Sensitivity

### Running cost, one row at a time

Each uncertain row is run at its low and then its high value, with every other row at its default, ignoring correlations. Rows are ranked by how much they move the difference (the baseline minus the option, positive when the option is cheaper to run). A table lists only the rows either combination’s running cost reads: capital costs, lifetimes and price changes are in the payback table below, the roof solar rows appear only with solar, and the control boost only on Cosy and Agile. The low and high are the ends of each row’s range, not percentiles; for the SPF they are the clip limits of its lognormal distribution, far out in its tails.

On the price cap, a kWh of heat costs almost the same from either system at the central values: 9.59p from the boiler (8.15p ÷ 0.85) and 9.50p from the heat pump (26.60p ÷ 2.8). So rows that change how much heat the house needs move both running costs but barely the difference, which turns on the SPF, the boiler efficiency and the gas standing charge the heat pump house doesn’t pay. The boiler’s pump and fan electricity (86 kWh a year) adds about £20 to the gas setups’ bills.

## Checks against outside references

### The Home Energy Model (HEM)

Each check compares annual **space heat** for the benchmark 1930s semi, described the same way on both sides, on the PVGIS typical year. The rules were committed before HEM ran: within 15%, proceed; 15–30%, build a two-node model; above 30%, stop and review. The engine’s tests guard each figure within 10%. See [the HEM runs](../scripts/benchmark/hem/README.md).

| Check | HEM | HEM air temperature when heating | Engine | Engine ÷ HEM − 1 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Heated in every hour, no thermal mass (phase 1, about 17.8 °C air) | 13,700 kWh | 17.8 °C | 13,000 kWh | −4.8% |
| The decision run: SAP’s periods (weekdays 7–9 am and 4–11 pm, weekends 7 am to 11 pm), 19.8 °C air | 13,600 kWh | 20.4 °C | 14,200 kWh | +4.3% |
| The heat pump’s schedule: 7 am to 11 pm every day, 19.8 °C air | 14,800 kWh | 20.1 °C | 14,500 kWh | −2.4% |
| A diagnostic: every hour, the same thermal mass, 19.8 °C air | 17,300 kWh | 19.8 °C | 15,900 kWh | −8.4% |

- **Decision:** on SAP’s periods the engine is +4.3% from HEM, inside 15%, so the one thermal-mass node proceeds. On the heat pump’s day it is −2.4%, also inside, so the heat pump may use that schedule.
- **The bias:** the difference between those two gaps is −6.7 points. On the two schedules the engine understates the heat pump’s space heat against the boiler’s by about that much, which favours the heat pump ([issue 15](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/15)).
- **The diagnostic** shows the one node’s error depends on the heating pattern: it stores daytime surplus more readily than HEM’s elements, so it falls below HEM when heated in every hour.

### PVGIS’s PV calculator

The reference system, fixed before PVcalc was called: 4 kWp in London, tilted 35° and facing south, with 14% system losses. PVcalc averages 2005–2023 and models the sky, module temperature and reflection in more detail than the engine, so the pre-registered tolerance is 8%.

| | Engine (typical year) | PVcalc |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Annual yield | 3,971 kWh | 4,075 kWh |
| Irradiation on the panel | 1,178 kWh/m² | 1,261 kWh/m² |

The engine is −2.6% from PVcalc: inside the 8% tolerance. See [scripts/pvgis/](../scripts/pvgis/) and [engine.md](../REFERENCE/engine.md#checks-against-outside-references).

## How the ranges are made

- **Samples:** 500 joint samples with seed 1, shared by all 10 combinations. Each sample draws a value for every uncertain row: Fabric quality factor (one multiplier on every U-value and the air change rate); Internal gains per occupant; Heat pump space heating flow temperature at the design outdoor temperature; Heat pump space heating flow temperature at the mild outdoor temperature; Control boost: how far the setpoint rises in cheap hours and falls in peak hours, heat pump on a time-of-use tariff; Heating setpoint: air temperature during heating periods (calibrated to measured gas use); Gas combi boiler seasonal efficiency (space heat and hot water); Air source heat pump seasonal performance factor (space heat and hot water combined); Heat pump standby electricity, as a share of its yearly electricity (field trial); Hot water use per occupant; Export rate for solar setups, flat, London; Base electricity use (lights and appliances), the same in both setups; Roof solar PV system size before the roof limit; Share of one roof slope that panels can cover; Roof solar PV direction; Replacement gas combi boiler, installed; Air source heat pump, installed, with its cylinder and typical radiator changes, before the grant; Roof solar PV system, installed, per kWp; Gas combi boiler lifetime; Air source heat pump lifetime; Roof solar PV system lifetime; Real change in gas prices each year, after inflation; Real change in electricity prices each year, after inflation. Every other number is fixed.
- **Stable draws:** each value comes from a hash of the seed, the sample number and the row id, passed through the row’s inverse distribution function. Triangular rows use their default as the mode. The SPF is lognormal and clipped to its low and high.
- **Central** is the run with every row at its default. **Median** and the **10th to 90th percentile** come from the samples (linear interpolation between ranked samples).
- **Fabric quality** is one shared factor on every U-value and the air change rate.
- **Correlated rows:** a Gaussian copula correlates, in normal-score space, internal gains and hot water use per occupant (0.5); and the gas and electricity real price changes (0.6). The other rows are drawn independently of each other.
- **Rounding:** costs to £10, energy to 100 kWh, carbon to 10 kg, shares to 5% and payback to whole years.

## Conventions

- **Time base:** the engine steps through the PVGIS typical year in UTC hours. Schedules and tariff periods are in UK local time, converted with the UK clock-change rule applied to 2026. The typical year’s months come from different years, so its weekdays are taken from 2026: 1 January is a Thursday, and the clock changes fall on Sundays ([issue 25](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/25)). Agile’s past rates are placed on the typical year by calendar date and time, with 29 February dropped.
- **Carbon:** imported electricity at the annual average grid factor and gas at its combustion factor. Exported solar electricity earns no carbon credit ([issue 34](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/34)).
- **Payback is undiscounted,** in today’s money with a real price change for each fuel ([issue 37](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/37)).
- **The boiler needs replacing now.** Every setup is compared with replacing it like for like, so a heat pump only has to recover its extra cost over a new boiler. A home with years left in its boiler would see later payback ([issue 37](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/37)).
- **The grant and MCS:** the £7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme grant applies to the heat pump’s first installation only, and the heat pump and PV are assumed MCS-certified, which the grant and export payments need. The PV inverter is not replaced within PV’s lifetime ([issue 39](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/39)).

## Limitations

- **One calibrated setpoint applies to every setup.** It comes from gas-heated homes. The heat pump’s longer day comes from SAP, not field data, and on the two schedules the engine understates the heat pump’s space heat by about 6.7 points against the boiler’s ([issue 15](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/15)). The setpoint may also absorb errors in the default U-values ([issue 14](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/14)).
- **One thermal-mass node** holds the air and the fabric at one temperature. Against HEM it is 4.3% high on SAP’s periods, 2.4% low on the heat pump’s day and 8.4% low when heated in every hour.
- **The heat pump’s hourly COP follows a curve scaled to the sampled SPF** on the price cap and the gas schedule; its own schedule and control then change its efficiency through the curve. Its output cap is a simple limit, not a sizing method, and it has no backup heater. Its standby is a share of its electricity, so small houses get less of it.
- **Time-of-use results assume a smart controller** and value none of the extra warmth control buys; Agile is one past year on typical weather (see the time-of-use caveats).
- **One typical weather year and one location** ([issue 16](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/16)), and an **annual average grid carbon factor** ([issue 17](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/17)).
- **Geometry and fabric are estimates by age band:** window areas use the RdSAP 2012 formula ([issue 26](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/26)), the air change rate is an estimate by age band ([issue 27](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/27)), and the derived geometry has not been checked against an MCS heat loss calculation ([issue 24](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/24)).
- **Only two pairs of rows are correlated:** the per-occupant gains and hot water terms, and the gas and electricity price changes. Both coefficients are estimates. Every other uncertain row is drawn independently.
- **Constant internal gains**, and windows split equally over four orientations.
- **Not validated against real homes yet.** The site launches as a beta; volunteer homes and expert review follow.
